title: Diverse computational systems emulate each other with comparable step counts

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Diverse computational systems emulate each other with comparable step counts

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Almost all the varied systems considered (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution and other systems) can emulate each other in a comparable number of steps, typically with at most polynomial overhead such as t^2 or t^(d+1), so rates of computation do not differ greatly across systems, including presumably those in nature.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: almost all the very varied systems in this book can actually be made to emulate each other in a quite comparable number of steps.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Undecidability and Intractability” (from p. 753), p. 765. Scope: cellular automata, Turing machines, register machines, substitution systems and other simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-25: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Simulation overheads among specific abstract models are mathematically resolvable and much public work exists. The broad prevalence assertion and physical extension cannot be inferred from those pairwise constructions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each named formalism, construct uniform simulations of the others and prove time-overhead bounds as functions of simulated time and dimension. Superpolynomial lower bounds or failure of a claimed simulation refute a pairwise assertion; polynomial constructions confirm it for the covered formalisms.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
"Almost all" formalisms are not enumerated.

Overhead depends on encoding and cost conventions.

The extension to systems in nature lacks validated digital models.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.45
data existence: 0.75
discriminating power: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.5

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The explicit emulations, including a Turing machine using on the order of t squared steps to match t steps of a cellular automaton, are finite constructions a simulator can check. The sentence then says almost all of the varied systems, and presumably those in nature, have comparable rates. A handful of constructions does not settle that extension, and no dataset measures computational rate across natural processes.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each published emulation, such as a Turing machine rebuilding t steps of a one-dimensional cellular automaton in order t squared steps, simulate both systems and compare step counts. A verified polynomial emulation supports that pair; a forced exponential emulation of a simple universal system would challenge the general claim for that pair.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Almost all systems, and systems in nature, lie beyond the explicit constructions.

Asking about existence over many paths is the separate P versus NP question.

A polynomial overhead in one encoding leaves other encodings and other features of the output open.
